newsitem.title: USA: SMOKE TRIAL JUDGE BARS MISSING LETTER TESTIMONY.
newsitem.headline: SMOKE TRIAL JUDGE BARS MISSING LETTER TESTIMONY.

text.p: The judge in a $5 billion secondhand-smoke trial on Thursday barred former U.S. Surgeon General Jesse Steinfeld from testifying about a letter written to President Nixon by an R.J. Reynolds Tobacco chief executive in 1972 that anti-tobacco lawyers allege led to Steinfeld's dismissal for his anti-smoking policies.

The letter, reportedly written shortly before Nixon's landslide re-election, is missing. Rival lawyers said Steinfeld was unable to locate his own copy of the Reynolds letter, a search of the late Nixon's archives had proven fruitless, and Reynolds was unable to find a copy of the letter.

According to lawyers representing 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants suing U.S. cigarette companies, Steinfeld was given the Reynolds letter in October, 1972, to draft a response. The letter, plaintiffs' lawyer Stanley Rosenblatt said, reminded Nixon of Reynolds' cash contributions to his re-election campaign and a verbal promise to fire Steinfeld.

Steinfeld, the first surgeon general to propose limits on smoking in public places out of fears secondhand smoke was injuring non-smokers, was asked to resign shortly after the election in November, 1972, Rosenblatt said.
"This is total hearsay ... hearsay upon hearsay," said Hugh Whiting, an attorney for Reynolds, urging Judge Robert Kaye of Dade County Court to forbid testimony on the missing letter.
Kaye said the letter's existence could not be sufficiently proven but allowed Rosenblatt to question Steinfeld about other government memoranda and letters referring to the missing Reynolds letter.
